topic: Reformer terms explained: springs, footbar and carriage

slides.headline: New to the reformer? Learn the lingo
slides.sub: Carriage, springs, footbar, straps and headrest, in plain English.

slides.title: The carriage: the bit that moves
slides.body: The padded platform you lie, kneel or sit on is the carriage. It slides along rails, and your job is usually to control it on the way out and, just as importantly, on the way back in.

slides.title: Springs: heavier isn't always harder
slides.body: Springs add resistance, but heavier springs can make some exercises easier by giving you more support. Lighter springs often ask for more control. Your instructor chooses them to suit your body and goals.

slides.title: The footbar: your base
slides.body: The padded bar at the end is where your feet or hands push. It can usually be raised or lowered. Heels, arches or toes on the bar change which muscles work the hardest.

slides.title: Straps, headrest and shoulder rests
slides.body: Straps connect your hands or feet to the springs for pulling and leg work. The headrest adjusts for neck comfort, and shoulder rests stop you sliding off the end during pushing exercises.

slides.title: Getting on and off safely
slides.body: Check the carriage is still and the springs are secure before you climb on or off, and ask your instructor to show you how. Moving slowly and with control is part of the exercise too.

slides.headline: Want a guided first session?
slides.body: Our clinical Pilates team starts with an assessment, then shows you around the reformer at a pace that suits you. Book online, link in bio.

caption:
Carriage, springs, footbar... is the reformer speaking a different language?

The carriage is the sliding platform you lie or kneel on. Springs add resistance, but more springs can actually make some moves easier by giving you support. The footbar is your base for pushing, and the straps link your hands or feet to the springs for pulling.

Knowing the terms makes cues easier to follow, so you can focus on moving well instead of wondering what 'two reds and a blue' means.
